title: Shapes and Contracts

post.author: u/glue_and_gesso_jurgita
post.title: I'm the night maker at a puppet workshop. At 02:10 the log said our three paper shadow puppets had been washed. They hang in the glass case, dry.

blocks.text: Thimbleby Puppet Works makes and mends puppets. I'm the night maker: I carve, sew and glue while the town sleeps. Our owner, Amarantha, wrote the workshop's care software herself, in Python, a language for writing programs.

In her code, each kind of puppet has a pattern that says what every puppet of that kind can do, like a blank form. That pattern is called a class. Each real puppet is an object: one filled-in copy of the form.
Something a class can do is a method, a named set of steps, like wash().

Amarantha wrote one class, Puppet, with wash() in it, and three kinds beneath it. A class built on another is a subclass. It inherits, gets for free, every method of the class above it; that is inheritance.

Here is the code. class Marionette(Puppet) means Marionette is a subclass of Puppet, and ... means nothing added. care_sheet.add puts a line on tomorrow's printed care sheet, log writes a line in the maintenance log, self is the puppet the method was called on, the f before the quotes fills in its name, and # starts a note:

class Puppet:
    def wash(self):
        care_sheet.add(self.name, "wash, warm water, 10 min")
        log(f"{self.name} washed")
class Marionette(Puppet): ...
class GloveFigure(Puppet): ...
class ShadowPuppet(Puppet): ...     # paper
for p in puppets: p.wash()          # night batch, 02:00

The last line is the night batch, a job that runs by itself at 02:00. It goes in steps. First it takes the next puppet due a clean. Then it calls that puppet's wash(), which adds the line to the sheet and writes "washed" in the log. Then it moves on. Nobody washes anything at night. The batch only writes. Radek, our morning restorer, starts at 07:30 and does exactly what the sheet says.
This spring we made our first shadow puppets, cut from oiled paper: the heron, the lantern-bearer and the moon. Water would ruin them. ShadowPuppet is a subclass of Puppet, so they got wash() too.
Tonight all ten puppets were due a clean. At 02:10 I read the maintenance log. Each line shows the time, the puppet, and what the log says happened:

02:00:03  goose           washed
02:00:04  heron           washed
02:00:05  lantern-bearer  washed
02:00:06  moon            washed
02:00:07  pedlar          washed
The sink is dry. I walked to the glass case. All three hang there, dry and untouched, and tomorrow's sheet says "wash, warm water, 10 min" beside each.
The log says the paper was washed. The paper says it wasn't.
I've crossed out three lines on the sheet in pen. Amarantha reads this in the morning. What should she change before tomorrow night?

Three subclasses inherit it: Marionette, 4 cloth puppets, washed; GloveFigure, 3 cloth puppets, washed; ShadowPuppet, 3 paper puppets, the heron, the lantern-bearer and the moon, logged as washed.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Amarantha's form picture is a good one. Here's the next idea. A method is a promise: anything with wash() says "you can wash me." The set of promises an object makes, the methods other code may call on it, is its interface. Think of the buttons on a lift: you press them without seeing the wires. A subclass inherits the promises along with the steps, whether it can keep them or not. There's a rule for that, called substitutability: anywhere the code expects a Puppet, any subclass should be able to stand in and keep every promise. A subclass can also override a method: write its own version with the same name, which runs instead of the one above it. So, questions. Which of your puppets can keep the wash() promise? Is there anything the paper ones can have done to them? And who calls wash(): only the batch, or something else too?

replies.author: u/glue_and_gesso_jurgita
replies.text: Amarantha says the paper ones get dusted with a soft dry brush. Only the batch calls wash() today, but Radek's tablet is getting a Wash now button. And for the winter show she's planning two new puppets: the crane, a marionette cut from paper, and the swan, a shadow puppet made of silk that can go in the sink.

comments.author: u/just_check_kunigunde
comments.text: One isinstance check and you're done. Don't redesign a class tree at 2 a.m. A puppet's type is the class it was made from. isinstance(p, ShadowPuppet) asks Python whether p was made from ShadowPuppet or one of its subclasses. Put if isinstance(p, ShadowPuppet): continue in the batch, where continue means skip to the next puppet. One line, working by breakfast. I've patched bigger trees than yours this way.

comments.author: u/fail_loud_wojciech
comments.text: A quiet fix is how you got here. Make it loud. In ShadowPuppet, override wash() so it raises an error. raise stops the method at once and throws out an exception, an error message that climbs back up through the code that called it. If nothing catches it, the program stops. Then nobody can ever put paper down for washing by accident again: the batch will refuse.

reply.prompt: Tomorrow night the batch runs again at 02:00. What should Amarantha change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Override wash() in ShadowPuppet to do nothing, so the night batch passes paper puppets by.
options.verdict: No false lines, no care, no word
options.part2: Amarantha gave ShadowPuppet its own wash() with one word in it, pass, Python's way of saying do nothing. The next night the log had 7 washed lines and the sheet 7, with no false line. But the heron, the lantern-bearer and the moon got nothing: no dusting, no line on the sheet, no word in the log. wash() still said yes, and quietly did nothing. In November the crane arrived, class PaperMarionette(Marionette). It inherited Marionette's wash(), and at 02:00:02 the log said "crane washed": 1 false line, and paper on Radek's sheet again. The silk swan, class SilkShadow(ShadowPuppet), inherited the empty override instead: a puppet that can be washed, and never was. That made 4 puppets left without care and nothing said.
options.senior: An empty override keeps the promise's name and breaks its meaning. Callers still believe wash() means washed, and nothing tells them otherwise, so the failure goes silent instead of false. It also fixes one class, not the idea: a paper puppet under another parent inherits the old wash(), and a washable puppet under ShadowPuppet inherits the empty one. The subclass still can't stand in for its parent; it just hides that it can't.

options.text: Give each puppet a list of the care steps it can take, and have the batch run only those.
options.part2: Amarantha took wash() out of Puppet. She wrote two care steps, small classes with one method each, run(): Wash adds "wash, warm water, 10 min" and DryBrush adds "dry brush, soft bristles". Each puppet is now made with a list of the steps it can take, and the batch runs only those. The next night: 10 lines on the sheet, 7 washes and 3 dry brushings, 0 false lines, and 10 of 10 puppets given care that suits them. Radek's Wash now button runs the same list. In November the crane was made with [DryBrush()]: 11 of 11. Replayed with the swan instead, made with [Wash()]: 11 of 11 again. Nothing in the batch had to change.
options.senior: This is composition: an object holds the parts that do the work, instead of getting them from a parent class. Each care step keeps one small promise, run(), and each puppet holds only the steps it can really take, so no puppet carries a promise it can't keep. A new kind of puppet needs a list, not a change to the tree or the batch. Gamma and his co-authors put it as "Favor object composition over class inheritance." The cost: someone must choose each new puppet's list, so make leaving it out an error.

options.text: Have the night batch check each puppet's type, and skip ShadowPuppet before it calls wash().
options.part2: Amarantha added one line to the batch, if isinstance(p, ShadowPuppet): continue, and had it write "skipped (ShadowPuppet)" in the log. The next night: 7 washed lines, 3 honest skips, 0 false. But the paper puppets got no dusting either: 7 of 10 given care that suits them. Radek's Wash now button needed its own copy of the check. In November the crane, a PaperMarionette, is not a ShadowPuppet, so it slipped past the check, and the log said "crane washed": 1 false line. The swan, washable silk, is a ShadowPuppet, so it was skipped: 7 of 11.
options.senior: A type check asks what class an object is when the real question is what it can take. Class and material don't line up, so the check is wrong for the paper marionette and the silk shadow puppet. And it spreads: every caller of wash() needs the same check, and every new kind means finding and editing all of them. Checks like this are often a sign that a class is carrying a promise it can't keep.

options.text: Make wash() raise an error in ShadowPuppet, so a wrong call stops the night batch at once.
options.verdict: Honest, and it stops everyone's care
options.part2: Amarantha made ShadowPuppet's wash() raise NotImplementedError, Python's error for a step a class can't do. The next night the batch washed the baker, the fiddler and the goose, reached the heron at 02:00:04 and stopped. 3 lines on the sheet, 0 false, and the 6 puppets after the heron got no care at all: 3 of 10 given care that suits them. It stopped there every night after. With the crane in the list, it came second, before the heron: "crane washed", 1 false line, then the stop.
options.senior: Failing loudly beats a false log: nobody reads a lie as the truth. But it puts the error on every puppet that happens to come after the paper ones, and the subclass still breaks its parent's promise; it just refuses out loud. You could catch the error for each puppet and carry on, but then the batch is quietly sorting puppets by what they can't do. Better to stop promising wash() to things that can't be washed.

sim.title: Replay the night batch at Thimbleby
sim.lede: You're Amarantha, replaying tonight from 02:00:00, before the night batch. Ten puppets are due a clean, taken in name order, one a second: the baker, the fiddler, the goose, the heron, the lantern-bearer, the moon, the pedlar, the ploughman, the queen and the wolf. The heron, the lantern-bearer and the moon are paper ShadowPuppets; the rest are cloth. Nobody washes anything at night: each step only adds a line to tomorrow's care sheet and the maintenance log. Pick how care is coded: inheritance as built; an empty override in ShadowPuppet; a type check in the batch; wash() raising an error in ShadowPuppet; or composed care steps, where each puppet is made with its own list of steps (Wash for cloth and silk, DryBrush for paper). Then add a new kind to test the design: the crane, a paper marionette, class PaperMarionette(Marionette), or the swan, a silk shadow puppet that can be washed, class SilkShadow(ShadowPuppet). A false line is a "washed" line for a paper puppet. Changing a setting rewinds to 02:00:00; press Next puppet or Run to 02:10.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Next puppet four times. At 02:00:04 the heron is "washed": the first false line. Press Run to 02:10: 10 lines on the care sheet, 3 false, care that suits 7 of 10. Add the crane: 4 false. Pick the empty override: 0 false, but 3 puppets left without care and nothing said; with the swan, 4. The type check: 0 false, until the crane slips past it, 1 false. wash() raising an error: the batch stops at the heron, 3 of 10 cared for. Composed care steps: 10 of 10, and 11 of 11 with the crane or the swan.

explain.oneLine: Nobody washed the paper. The night batch called wash() on every puppet, and ShadowPuppet had inherited wash() from Puppet, so the code wrote "washed" for three paper puppets it could never wash. The fix is to stop handing every puppet the same promise: give each one the care steps it can really take.

steps.title: Classes, objects and methods.
steps.text: A class is a pattern for a kind of thing: what it holds and what it can do. An object is one real thing made from that pattern, like one filled-in copy of a form. Making ten puppet objects from four classes gives ten copies, each with its own name. A method is something the class can do, such as wash(). When code writes p.wash(), Python goes in steps. First, it looks at which class p was made from. Next, it looks for wash() in that class. If it isn't there, it looks in the class above, and so on up the tree. Then it runs the first wash() it finds, with p as self. What can go wrong: the wash() it finds may have been written for a different kind of puppet.

steps.title: Inheritance hands down the steps and the promise.
steps.text: A subclass gets every method of the class above it, its parent. That saves writing wash() three times, and it is why the tree looked tidy. But a method is also a promise to the rest of the code: "you can wash me." ShadowPuppet inherited the promise along with the steps. The night batch trusted it, called wash() on the heron, the lantern-bearer and the moon, and each call did exactly what the code said: added "wash, warm water, 10 min" to the sheet and wrote "washed" in the log. The machine did nothing wrong. The record is false because the promise was false.

steps.title: Substitutability: a subclass must keep its parent's promises.
steps.text: The usual rule is that anywhere code expects a Puppet, any subclass should be able to stand in without surprising it. A paper puppet can't keep wash(), so ShadowPuppet can't stand in for Puppet, and every caller of wash() is at risk. The next case, The Five Rules of the Workshop, covers this rule in full. Here it is enough to see the trap: inheritance shares behaviour by the family tree, and the family tree is about what a thing is, not what it can take.

steps.title: The three patches move the problem.
steps.text: An empty override makes wash() say yes and do nothing: no false line, but no care and no word about it, and a paper puppet under another parent still inherits the old wash(). A type check in the batch skips ShadowPuppet: honest tonight, but it asks about the class instead of the material, so a paper marionette slips through and a washable silk shadow puppet is skipped, and every other caller needs the same check. Raising an error refuses loudly, but the batch stops at the first paper puppet and the six puppets after it get nothing. In the sim: 3 silent, 1 false with the crane, and 3 of 10 cared for.

steps.title: Composition: give each puppet the steps it can take.
steps.text: Take wash() out of Puppet. Write each care step as its own small class with one method, run(): Wash and DryBrush. That one method is the care step's interface, the only promise it makes. Each puppet is made with a list of the steps that suit it. The batch goes in steps. First, it takes the next puppet. Next, it takes each step in that puppet's list. Then it calls run() on the step, which adds the sheet line and the log line. Last, it moves on. Nothing is inherited that a puppet can't keep, and a new kind of puppet needs a list, not a change to the batch. What can go wrong: someone makes a new puppet with the wrong list, or none, so make an empty list an error.

diagram.aria: The fix. The night batch at 02:00 takes each puppet and runs its care list. The 7 cloth puppets carry a list with Wash, which adds wash, warm water, 10 min. The 3 paper puppets carry a list with DryBrush, which adds dry brush, soft bristles.

explain.caption: The fix. Puppet no longer has wash(). Each puppet carries a list of care steps, and the night batch runs only those: Wash for the 7 cloth puppets, DryBrush for the heron, the lantern-bearer and the moon. Replayed in the sim: 10 lines on the sheet, 0 false, 10 of 10 given care that suits them.

fix.title: The fix: composed care steps instead of an inherited wash()
fix.text: Remove wash() from Puppet. Write each care step as a small class with one method, run(puppet): Wash adds "wash, warm water, 10 min" and writes "washed"; DryBrush adds "dry brush, soft bristles" and writes "dry-brushed". Give every puppet a list of steps when it is made: [Wash()] for the cloth ones, [DryBrush()] for the heron, the lantern-bearer and the moon. Change the batch to run each puppet's list, and have Radek's Wash now button run the same list. Make a puppet with an empty or missing list an error, so nobody gets a care step by default. To pin the promise down, declare a CareStep base with run() marked abstract, so Python refuses to make a step that has no run(). In the sim: 10 of 10 tonight, 0 false lines, and 11 of 11 with the crane or the swan.

limits: Composition moves the choice to whoever makes each puppet. The crane is only right because someone gave it [DryBrush()]; a wrong list is still wrong, so check new kinds before their first night.
More small parts means more to read. Five puppets and two steps are easy; fifty kinds and twelve steps need names, a short guide and tests that each kind gets the steps you expect.
Inheritance still has a place. When every subclass truly keeps every promise, sharing code by inheritance is simpler. The trouble starts when a parent promises things only some children can do.

head: Design
Good
Bad

3 puppets silently get nothing; the crane is still washed; the swan never is.
One line; the log admits the skips.
Asks the class, not the material: the crane slips past, the swan is skipped; every caller needs a copy.
The batch stops at the heron: 3 of 10 cared for, every night.
10 of 10 tonight, 11 of 11 with either new kind; the batch never changes.
Someone must choose each puppet's list; more small parts to name.

explain.seniorTake: Inheritance shares two things at once: code and promises. The code is the easy part to see; the promises are the part that bites, because every caller trusts them. Use inheritance when every subclass can truly keep every promise of its parent, and say so in a short interface. When kinds differ in what they can do, compose: give each object the parts it can really use, and let the caller depend only on the small promise those parts make. Type checks and empty overrides are usually a sign that a promise was handed to something that can't keep it. Fix the promise, not each caller.

realWorld.title: Design Patterns, 1994: favor composition
realWorld.text: Erich Gamma is one of the four authors of Design Patterns. In a 2005 interview Bill Venners puts to Gamma the principle "you offer in the GoF introduction": "Favor object composition over class inheritance." Gamma answers: "Inheritance is a cool way to change behavior." And: "Composition has a nicer property." Then: "That's why you should favor composition."

realWorld.title: Gamma: composition still uses small interfaces
realWorld.text: In the same interview Gamma adds: "A common misunderstanding is that composition doesn't use inheritance at all. Composition is using inheritance, but typically you just implement a small interface and you do not inherit from a big class." Each care step here is that: a small class keeping one small promise, run().

realWorld.title: Gamma: an interface is the vocabulary
realWorld.text: On interfaces, Gamma says: "An interface distills the collaboration between objects." And: "An interface is free from implementation details, and it defines the vocabulary of the collaboration." He also warns that changing a published interface breaks the code that uses it: "Since changing interfaces breaks clients you should consider them as immutable once you've published them."

realWorld.title: The book's own words, as cited
realWorld.text: The Wikipedia article on the book cites it for "Program to an interface, not an implementation" and "Favor 'object composition' over 'class inheritance'", on pages 18 and 20, and for the reason inheritance is risky: "Because inheritance exposes a subclass to details of its parent's implementation".

realWorld.title: Python: classes, overriding and isinstance
realWorld.text: The Python tutorial: "Classes provide a means of bundling data and functionality together. Creating a new class creates a new type of object, allowing new instances of that type to be made." On inheritance: "Derived classes may override methods of their base classes." And: "Use isinstance() to check an instance's type".

realWorld.title: Python: abstract base classes enforce a promise
realWorld.text: Python's abc module provides "the infrastructure for defining abstract base classes (ABCs) in Python". Of a method marked abstract it says: "A class that has a metaclass derived from ABCMeta cannot be instantiated unless all of its abstract methods and properties are overridden." A CareStep base with an abstract run() makes Python refuse to create a step that doesn't keep its one promise.

realWorld.title: Python: protocols, promises checked by shape
realWorld.text: The typing module's Protocol is the "Base class for protocol classes." The documentation says: "Such classes are primarily used with static type checkers that recognize structural subtyping (static duck-typing)". A checker then accepts any class that has a run() method, without it inheriting from anything.

interview.answer: I start from what each object can actually do. Inheritance shares code and promises down a family tree, so it fits when every subclass can keep every promise of its parent: anywhere the parent is expected, the child can stand in without surprises. When kinds differ in what they can do, I prefer composition: the object holds small parts that do the work, and callers depend on the small interface those parts share. An interface is the set of promises an object makes, the methods other code may call, so callers can rely on what it does without knowing how. A story I'd tell: a base class had a step every subclass inherited, and a new subclass couldn't really do it. A nightly job called the step on everything, and the log said it was done for items it could never apply to. The quick patches were an empty override, which hid the failure, a type check, which spread to every caller and broke with the next kind, and raising an error, which stopped the whole job. The fix was to compose: each item carries the steps it can take, and the job runs only those. I'd make an empty list an error and use an abstract base class or a protocol so each step must have its one method. Inheritance still wins when the tree is small and the promises truly hold.

atWork: Look for a class tree where a base class does a step that every subclass inherits, and a scheduled job or a loop calls that step on everything. Payments and notifications are the usual places: a base Payment with refund(), and a new kind, such as a gift voucher, that can't be refunded to a card but inherited refund() anyway; or a base Notifier that sends a text and logs "sent", and a new kind of customer who has no phone number. It is a common pattern: the log says done for things the step could never apply to. Search your code for isinstance checks or empty overrides (methods whose body is pass or just returns): each one may mark a promise handed to a class that can't keep it. Could those steps be parts each object holds, with a small interface, instead of methods inherited from a big parent? Standards: none apply here; this is engineering work, not audit work.

recall.prompt: Your billing code has a class Payment with a refund() method that sends money back to the card and logs "refunded". CardPayment, BankTransfer and GiftVoucher are built on Payment. Vouchers can't be refunded to a card, but GiftVoucher gets refund() from Payment, and last night's refund job logged "refunded" for 12 vouchers that never got anything back. A colleague wants to add if isinstance(p, GiftVoucher): continue to the job and move on. What went wrong, and what would you do?

keyIdeas.idea: GiftVoucher inherited a promise, refund(), that it can't keep, so it can't stand in for Payment and the log says done when nothing happened
A type check works today but spreads to every caller and breaks with the next new kind
Compose instead: give each payment the refund steps it can really take, and have the job run only those

recall.model: GiftVoucher inherited refund() from Payment, and with it the promise that a voucher can be refunded to a card. It can't keep that promise, so it can't stand in for a Payment, and the job trusted it: the false log says refunded for 12 vouchers that got nothing. The isinstance check would hide tonight's problem, but it spreads: every caller of refund() needs its own copy, and every new kind of payment means finding them all again. I'd use composition instead: give each payment the refund steps it can really take, such as a card refund for cards and a credit note for vouchers, and have the job run only those steps. Then fix the 12 vouchers by hand and tell finance the log was wrong.

recall.prompt: Puppet has a wash() method. The code says class GloveFigure(Puppet): ... and nothing else. What happens when the night batch calls wash() on a GloveFigure?
options: Python raises an error, because GloveFigure has no wash() of its own
Python runs Puppet's wash(), because GloveFigure inherits it
Nothing happens, because ... means the class does nothing
Python asks which version to run, because two classes are involved
recall.why: A subclass gets every method of its parent. Python looks for wash() in GloveFigure, doesn't find it, looks in Puppet and runs that one, with the glove figure as self. The ... only means nothing was added to the class.

recall.prompt: A CareStep class is built with Python's abc module, and its run() method is marked abstract. Someone writes a DryBrush subclass but forgets to write run(). What happens?
options: DryBrush objects are made normally and run() does nothing
The night batch skips DryBrush steps and logs a warning
Python refuses to make a DryBrush object, because an abstract method isn't overridden
Python copies run() from another subclass of CareStep
recall.why: Python's documentation says a class whose metaclass comes from ABCMeta cannot be instantiated unless all of its abstract methods and properties are overridden. So the mistake shows up the moment someone tries to make a DryBrush, not at 02:00 in a log.

recall.prompt: To stop paper puppets being washed, ShadowPuppet overrides wash() with a body of pass. What is the main problem with this?
options: It makes the night batch slower, because every call now does two things
It still writes "washed" in the log for every paper puppet
wash() still promises washing but quietly does nothing, so paper puppets get no care and nothing says so
Python won't allow a subclass to override a method of its parent
recall.why: The override replaces Puppet's wash() entirely, so no line is written at all. The promise keeps its name and loses its meaning: callers think wash() means washed, the paper puppets get no dusting, and nothing in the log shows it. In the sim, 3 puppets are left without care and nothing said.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The care steps have worked all winter: no false lines. In February Amarantha got tired of typing lists, so she changed Puppet: any puppet made without a list now gets [Wash()] automatically. On Tuesday a volunteer added four rod puppets with wax heads for the spring show and gave them no list. At 02:00 the night batch wrote "washed" for all four, and Radek's sheet said "wash, warm water, 10 min" beside each. Wax goes soft in warm water. Radek noticed only because the heads looked new.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What went wrong, and how should new puppets get their care steps?

keyIdeas.idea: Handing every puppet [Wash()] when it has no list is inheritance's trap again: a promise the wax puppets never chose
Make each new puppet state its own steps: no list given, no puppet made
Catch a missing or doubtful list early: raise an error when a puppet is made without one, or flag new kinds before their first night

coldCase.model: It's the same trap as the paper puppets, back again in a new place. Giving every puppet [Wash()] when nobody chose a list works just like inheriting wash(): the wax puppets never chose that step, yet they carry the promise, and the batch trusted it. The point of the lists was that each puppet's care is a decision someone makes. So make it required: a puppet must give its own list when it is made, and Puppet should raise an error, and refuse to make the puppet, when the list is missing. If an empty list is ever right, write it out on purpose. Then flag every new kind of puppet for Radek or Amarantha to check before its first night, or add a test that each kind gets the steps you expect.
